segments.text: There are three types of compressed gases, liquefied gases, non-liquefied gases, and
dissolved gases.
Liquefied gases are those that, under the right conditions, can become liquid inside
the pressurized cylinders.
Some common examples are chlorine, carbon dioxide, liquefied petroleum gas, and liquefied
nitrous gas.
On the flip side, non-liquefied gases stay in a gas state regardless of the temperature.
They are sometimes called pressurized gases and include nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide,
and helium.
Compressed gases are very volatile as they need to be dissolved in a liquid phase solvent
to be stabilized.
The most common example is acetylene, which needs to be stored in the cylinder fully packed
with a filter, saturated in acetone to prevent explosions.
Due to the various hazards associated with the different types of compressed gases, cylinders
should always be clearly labeled.
Compressed gas cylinders also come in different designs and shapes based on the type and
pressure of their contents.
There are three main types, high pressure cylinders, low pressure cylinders, and cryogenic
containers.
High pressure cylinders are often tall and narrow with thick walls.
They are heavy even when empty and are usually made of steel or aluminum.
High pressure cylinders can withstand up to 10,000 psi and commonly hold gases like nitrogen,
helium, hydrogen, oxygen, and carbon dioxide.
Low pressure cylinders tend to be fatter and lighter with thin walls and welded seams.
Low pressure cylinders can withstand up to 500 psi and commonly hold liquefied petroleum
gases and refrigerant gases.
The last category is cryogenic containers, which typically operate at a pressure between
20 and 500 psi.
As the temperature increases, a relief valve is used to relieve pressure.
No matter the type of cylinder, they must always be supported.
This can be done through wall mounted brackets, chains, or anchors.
Anchoring systems must be able to support the weight of the cylinder once both empty
and full.
All piping systems used for flammable or toxic gases should meet OSHA, NFPA, and ANSI standards.
Pressure regulators and gauges need to be rated for the specific type of cylinder being
used and can't be adapted for other uses.
Due to the volatile nature of compressed gas, many hazards are associated with their use.
